content.p: Lawrence Bishnoi has been behind bars in India for roughly a decade, yet his name is attached to some of the most widely reported killings and threats in South Asia and its diaspora. Indian and US authorities allege that he heads a gang that runs extortion and killings from inside a prison cell, and Canada has listed that gang as a terrorist entity. He has not, in any of the reports consulted, been convicted of the offences that made him famous. He is a defendant and a suspect in dozens of cases, many of them untried, and his lawyer has disputed the central claim that he controls anything from jail.

What follows separates what has been charged from what has been proved. The charges are serious. In India the National Investigation Agency (NIA) has accused him under anti-terror law. In July 2026 a US federal indictment charged him with ordering the June 2023 assassination of a Sikh separatist in Canada. US prosecutors stated that an indictment is merely an allegation and that all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty. No page consulted reports a conviction of Bishnoi in any case.
content.h2: A law student in campus politics
content.p: Lawrence Bishnoi was born on 12 February 1993. The Tribune gives his home as Dhattaranwali village near Abohar in Punjab and says his father joined the Haryana Police as a constable in 1992 and left after five years to farm. The Indian Express, which says he was born Balkaran Brar, quotes a cousin saying the family was wealthy and that the father owns 110 acres. According to the paper, Bishnoi reportedly told Delhi Police that his aunt suggested the name Lawrence because it "sounded better".

He moved to Chandigarh and studied at DAV College before joining Panjab University, where he took an LLB. The Tribune reports that some of the earliest cases against him date from his student-union days, after he met Goldy Brar, who was then president of the student union. The Indian Express, drawing on the NIA chargesheet and a police dossier, traces the story to 2008 and a campus spat during an election campaign, after which, it says, police reports allege that he and seven others set fire to a rival campaigner's car; he and eight friends were arrested within ten days. The paper reports that 18 of the 84 cases registered against him since 2008 were filed while he was a student, and that several early cases were quashed after the parties reached a compromise.

In 2010 he lost a bid to head the Student Organisation of Panjab University and, the paper says, allegedly assaulted his rival. He stood again in 2011 and won. A police officer quoted by the paper says that by 2013 he was backing another candidate and that, during that campaign, he and his associates allegedly killed a rival nominee. The Mob Museum, drawing on Jupinderjit Singh, author of the book Gangs of Punjab, puts it more simply: the group "started with student politics" and, when they could not win elections, "started bullying people and eventually formed a gang".
content.h2: Arrest and the years in custody
content.p: Accounts of when he was first locked up for good do not match. The Indian Express says he was caught at a police picket in 2014 on his way to a temple in Rajasthan. The Hindu says he has been in custody since January 2015. Republic World writes that he has been in jail since 2015, the Tribune in 2026 says 2017, and CBC says 2014. The Indian Express adds that he got away from police during a court appearance in 2015, allegedly to avenge a cousin's murder, and was later picked up in Fazilka. The Mob Museum places his recapture two months after the escape, south of Delhi.

His movements since then have been between prisons. The Tribune says he was brought to Delhi's Tihar Jail in 2021 over a case brought under the Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act, and that he has been in Gujarat's Sabarmati jail since 2023, where he is reported to be in isolation. Republic World says the authorities moved him between prisons because of concerns for his safety and his ability to get round jail rules.

In 2020 the Tribune reported that Chandigarh police had brought him on a production warrant over the murder of Sonu Shah, a property dealer with a criminal record who was shot in his Burail office on 28 September of the year before the report. The paper said that Bishnoi had confessed to hatching a murder conspiracy from jail and that questioning had shown he used a mobile phone to reach gang members. It also reported that shots were fired earlier that year at a businessman's house and a liquor store in the city at his behest, without saying who established this. These are police claims reported by the paper; the pages consulted do not give the outcome of any trial.
content.h2: The gang and its alleged reach
content.p: The Tribune in 2022 called him the ringleader of a 700-member gang operating across Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Delhi and Himachal Pradesh, with an international network, and said it extorted money from the liquor trade, Punjabi singers and other influential people. The NIA's chargesheet, according to The Indian Express, uses the same figure and says 300 of the 700 are from Punjab. The agency compared his rise to that of the fugitive gangster Dawood Ibrahim.

Bishnoi's advocate, Rajani, rejected this to The Indian Express: no phone had been recovered from Bishnoi in jail, she said, and no agency had established how he communicated. Republic World quoted the same lawyer as saying he was contesting about 40 criminal cases, including murder, extortion and terrorism charges, with many trials not yet begun. The Mob Museum notes that he gave video interviews on national television from custody, and quotes the reporter Ritesh Lakhi describing a businessman in California who received a video call from Bishnoi, supposedly in jail in Gujarat. Republic World adds that in one interview Bishnoi denied being "anti-national" and said he opposed the Khalistan movement; the video was later taken down and police were examining its origins.

The Indian Express says police believe Bishnoi and another gangster, Kala Jathedi, were allied for a time and that together their gangs committed more than 30 murders in Delhi, Punjab, Rajasthan and Haryana. It says the two have since fallen out. That figure is the police's claim as relayed by the paper, not a court finding.

The gang's public notoriety rests partly on its hostility to the film star Salman Khan. In 1998 Khan was accused of poaching blackbuck, an antelope that the Bishnoi community, which Lawrence Bishnoi belongs to, holds sacred. The Mob Museum says the case dragged on for decades and that in 2018 Bishnoi publicly threatened to kill the actor. The Hindu says there was a threatening email to Khan's office in March 2023, after which police registered a case against Bishnoi and others.

The Indian Express says police say they had not realised until they stumbled on this how closely the gang had been monitoring the actor: police on the trail of a murder accused described as a Bishnoi associate found in 2021 that he had turned up at a horse auction at which a representative of Khan was the second-highest bidder. In April 2024 two men fired shots in front of Khan's Mumbai home. The Wire said Anmol Bishnoi purportedly claimed responsibility in a Facebook post and that both Bishnoi brothers were reportedly named in the chargesheet. Anuj Thapan, who had been arrested over the firing, died in police custody on 1 May 2024; The Hindu says it is reported to have been suicide.

Sidhu Moose Wala, a 28-year-old Punjabi rap star, was shot dead in his SUV near his Punjab village in May 2022. Goldy Brar, living in Canada, claimed responsibility on Facebook hours later. The Mob Museum, quoting Lakhi, says the reasons the gang gave included the 2021 killing of a close friend of both men, Vicky Middukhera, and Moose Wala's supposed role in the killing of Brar's brother, though Lakhi said they had not been able to link him directly with those killings. The Hindu says that Brar's cousin Gurlal Brar was killed in Chandigarh in October 2020 and that the gang allegedly killed a Youth Congress leader, Gurlal Singh Pehalwan, in retaliation in February 2021.

The NIA has attributed the Moose Wala killing to Bishnoi's group, according to Republic World. A Punjab Police special investigation team said in 2023 that Anmol Bishnoi was a conspirator. The Tribune reported in 2022 that Delhi Police and Punjab Police had arrested more than a dozen gangsters over the killing, and that the NIA had questioned several Punjabi singers about the gang.

On 12 October 2024 Baba Siddique, a former Maharashtra minister and a friend of Khan, was shot dead in Mumbai. The Hindu reported that a Facebook post attributed to Shubu Lonkar, described as an alleged aide of Bishnoi, claimed responsibility and tied the killing to Thapan's death. The Tribune says three assailants shot Siddique. The Hindu also says the gang had claimed the September 2023 killing of Sukhdool Singh in Winnipeg, Canada, and the December 2023 killing of Sukhdev Singh Godamedi in Jodhpur, which it says was allegedly the work of the same gang.

The NIA registered its case in August 2022 against nine accused, including Lawrence and Anmol Bishnoi, Kala Jathedi and Goldy Brar. The Tribune says the case, under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, alleges a conspiracy to carry out terrorist activities in Delhi and elsewhere, and quotes the agency as saying some of the gangsters were in jail while others were operating from places including Canada, Pakistan, Malaysia, Australia and the UAE.

The agency arrested Bishnoi in its own case in late November 2022. A Delhi court granted it four more days of custody on 3 December that year after the agency had asked for ten. The NIA said then that the gang was raising funds through drug and weapons smuggling and extortion, and that most of its conspiracies were hatched inside jail by Bishnoi. In March 2023 it filed a 128-page chargesheet against him and 15 others. Republic World says that chargesheet details smuggling of weapons, explosives and drugs from Pakistan, and that the NIA links him with the banned Babbar Khalsa International. Those are the agency's claims. The pages consulted do not report a verdict.

His younger brother Anmol had been absconding since 2022. The NIA chargesheeted him in March 2023, saying he had aided Goldy Brar and Lawrence Bishnoi with acts of terrorism. A reward of 10 lakh rupees was offered for his arrest. Mumbai police began the extradition process in October 2024 after US officials told India he was in America. He was detained in the US in June 2025 and removed on 18 November 2025. He landed in India the next day, was arrested by the NIA as the 19th person held in the case and was sent to 11 days of custody by a Delhi court, which gave the agency less than the 15 it had asked for. According to officials quoted by The Tribune he faces at least 18 criminal cases. His first case, under the Arms Act, was registered in 2012 when he was 15.

In October 2024 the Royal Canadian Mounted Police said the Bishnoi group was connected to agents of the Government of India and was targeting people linked to the pro-Khalistan movement in Canada. India rejected this as preposterous, and Canada and India each expelled six diplomats. Republic World notes that Canada had not listed specific charges against Bishnoi at the time.

On 29 September 2025 Canada listed the Bishnoi Gang as a terrorist entity, a step that lets it freeze assets and bar entry. Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said the group had targeted communities for terror, violence and intimidation. Canada's World Sikh Organization called the listing an important first step; the Sikh Federation called it insufficient.

On 7 July 2026 a federal indictment was unsealed in Los Angeles. US prosecutors said Bishnoi and Brar were charged with ordering the 18 June 2023 shooting of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, a 45-year-old Canadian citizen, outside a Sikh temple in Surrey, British Columbia. The Mob Museum says that, according to the indictment, they provided the killers with a photograph of the target. According to the Justice Department, as reported by the Shillong Times (PTI), Bishnoi had delegated his enterprise to lieutenants: Brar for North America and Rohit Godara for Europe. The indictment alleged that Bishnoi, Brar and Godara extorted victims over encrypted messaging apps and that Bishnoi claimed responsibility in November 2023 for a shooting at the Vancouver home of a prominent Indian actor and singer.

The Justice Department said Bishnoi directed associates from his cell through contraband phones and internet devices to commit assassinations, shootings, extortion, kidnappings and drug trafficking, and that he and others tried to extort $5 million from victims in the Los Angeles area in December 2025 and January 2026. The case was part of Operation Hard Ball, in which 24 people were arrested in the US, Canada and Europe and 37 were charged in three indictments. The two other groups included one led by Jaggu Bhagwanpuria, whom the Mob Museum describes as a former Bishnoi lieutenant who split off.

The Shillong Times reported that the FBI announced a reward of $50,000 for Brar. On 28 September 2026 the FBI added Brar to its most-wanted list, raised the reward to $1 million and said he is believed to live in California and parts of Canada. The Tribune noted that the US allegation raises the question of how Bishnoi could use phones and messaging apps in a Gujarat jail, and that the NIA had made similar claims four years earlier.

India has dismissed Canada's allegations of a link to its agents. The Indian Eye reports that ties have since improved under Mark Carney, Canada's current prime minister, and that Ottawa has indicated it no longer connects India with crime inside Canada.
